artifact.canonical_name: IEEE Std 802.1DG-2025 — Time-Sensitive Networking Profile for Automotive In-Vehicle Ethernet Communications

sources.title: P802.1DG – TSN Profile for Automotive In-Vehicle Ethernet Communications
sources.role: Official IEEE 802.1 project page establishing scope, publication status, approval/publication dates and project history.

sources.title: Publication: IEEE 802.1DG-2025 Time-Sensitive Networking Profile for Automotive In-Vehicle Ethernet Communications
sources.role: Official IEEE 802.1 publication announcement summarizing automotive TSN profile purpose and applicability.

claims.text: IEEE 802.1DG is a published 2025 standard; the project page records Board approval on 2025-05-28 and publication on 2025-06-06.
claims.context: Status/date evidence from the IEEE 802.1 project page.

claims.text: The standard defines an automotive in-vehicle Ethernet TSN profile for bridged IEEE 802.3 networks, addressing deterministic/bounded latency and selecting applicable IEEE 802.1 TSN/security features for automotive use.
claims.context: Publicly stated standard scope; detailed normative parameters were not inspected.

claims.text: The public IEEE summary positions 802.1DG as guidance for automotive vendors/suppliers designing in-vehicle networks with bounded latency, bandwidth and synchronization requirements.
claims.context: Architecture relevance follows the standard’s stated profile purpose.

limitations.text: This verification used public IEEE project/publication pages; detailed normative requirements and parameter values in the full standard were not independently inspected.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on ieee-8021dg-automotive-tsn; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: Official IEEE 802.1 pages establish published-standard status, approval/publication dates, and the automotive TSN profile scope. Detailed normative contents remain outside this verification.

unresolved_questions: Which detailed mandatory/optional TSN feature selections and configuration parameters are normative in the full IEEE Std 802.1DG-2025 text?

editorial.why_now_note: Publication in 2025 places a formal automotive TSN profile inside the 2023-2026 E/E transition window.
editorial.rationale: A published automotive-specific TSN profile is directly relevant to deterministic Ethernet as the network substrate for centralized/zonal E/E architectures.

sources.title: CAN XL: CAN in Automation (CiA)
sources.role: Official CiA technical knowledge page establishing protocol properties, intended network role and ISO 11898-1:2024 standardization status.

claims.text: The CiA page describes CAN XL as the third generation of the CAN data link layer with a data-field length from 1 to 2048 bytes.
claims.context: Protocol characteristics stated by the relevant CAN industry association.

claims.text: CiA states that CAN XL is intended for backbone and sub-backbone network applications and is designed for integration into TCP/IP network systems.
claims.context: Architecture role stated on the official technical page.

claims.text: CiA states that CAN XL is standardized in ISO 11898-1:2024 and lists CiA 610–613 document series for related specifications, services and guidance.
claims.context: Public standardization/status metadata; inaccessible ISO normative text was not reconstructed.

claims.text: The page states that optional PWM coding can support bit rates of 20 Mbit/s and higher depending on physical network design.
claims.context: Public protocol capability statement with an explicit physical-network dependency.

limitations.text: The ISO 11898-1:2024 normative text was not available through the pinned Source Intake; this card verifies only the public CiA description and standardization status.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on cia-can-xl; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The pinned CiA page directly establishes CAN XL scope, public protocol characteristics, backbone/sub-backbone intent and ISO 11898-1:2024 status; detailed normative clauses remain outside this evidence.

editorial.why_now_note: CAN XL provides an important non-Ethernet high-bandwidth backbone/sub-backbone path in the 2023-2026 architecture transition.
editorial.rationale: It is a directly architecture-relevant in-vehicle network technology whose public specification status and intended role can be separated cleanly from unavailable normative detail.

artifact.canonical_name: OPEN Alliance TC14 10BASE-T1S automotive specification suite

sources.title: TC14 – Interoperability & Compliance Tests for 10BASE-T1S PHYs
sources.role: Official OPEN Alliance committee page and roadmap snapshot for automotive 10BASE-T1S conformance/interoperability specifications.

claims.text: OPEN Alliance TC14 states that its goal is enabling 10BASE-T1S in an automotive context through conformance, interoperability and EMC test specifications plus implementation/diagnostic work.
The committee scope includes PLCA registers, topology discovery, PMD transceiver interfaces, sleep/wake, and collaboration on ECU/channel/MACsec-related specifications.
The pinned roadmap lists multiple approved 2025-2026 specification/test-suite versions, including transceiver EMC, PLCA conformance and digPHY conformance deliverables.
claims.context: Roadmap status at pinned observation time.

limitations.text: The committee page establishes document scope/version status but does not by itself prove that a specific PHY/ECU product passes the conformance or interoperability suites.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on open-alliance-10base-t1s; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The official committee page verifies an automotive 10BASE-T1S specification/conformance ecosystem and concrete 2025-2026 roadmap milestones.

editorial.why_now_note: 10BASE-T1S fills a lower-speed/multidrop Ethernet niche and its automotive interoperability ecosystem matters to zonal edge connectivity.
editorial.rationale: Useful physical/network-layer evidence distinct from higher-speed backbone TSN and CAN XL.

artifact.canonical_name: OPEN Alliance TC9 Automotive Ethernet Channel & Components specifications

sources.title: TC9 – Automotive Ethernet Channel & Components
sources.role: Official OPEN Alliance committee page used for cabling/channel requirements, test methodology scope and current focus.

claims.text: TC9 defines electrical requirements and test procedures for automotive Ethernet cabling channels and components, including cables, connectors and assemblies aligned with IEEE 802.3 link-segment requirements.
The committee states that its work covers automotive Ethernet speed grades on electrical media and develops generic measurement/test procedures for link-segment and component qualification.
The pinned page states current work includes 1000BASE-T1 over coaxial media and 25GBASE-T1, while the roadmap lists 10BASE-T1S channel/component requirements v1.1 from June 2025.

limitations.text: This page verifies channel/component specification activity and versions, not electrical performance of any particular production harness or connector implementation.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on open-alliance-channel-components; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The official page establishes physical-channel/component responsibilities and test methodology spanning multiple Automotive Ethernet media/speeds.

editorial.why_now_note: Physical link/channel specifications are an often-hidden but essential constraint on the move to Ethernet-centric zonal/backbone architectures.
editorial.rationale: Strong supporting candidate for the physical-network layer, especially to prevent the survey from treating Ethernet as a purely logical/software transition.

artifact.canonical_name: Negotiating strict latency limits for dynamic real-time services in vehicular time-sensitive networks
artifact.organization: TU Dresden / HAW Hamburg / TU Eindhoven

sources.title: Negotiating strict latency limits for dynamic real-time services in vehicular time-sensitive networks
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors propose a service-discovery/QoS negotiation mechanism that communicates application requirements to a central TSN controller, which performs admission/resource configuration using network-calculus delay budgets.

In the evaluated realistic IVN, the authors find the per-queue delay-budget/network-calculus reservation approach to be the only tested scheme that consistently enforces hard latency constraints; alternative interval-based approaches can misconfigure resources.
Real-time data transfer bypasses the controller after flows/reservations are established, while the controller remains a setup-time dependency and potential single point of failure.

metrics.name: setup/signaling duration with SOME/IP scatter
metrics.context: 450 subscriptions in the realistic-IVN simulation; negotiation without scatter is reported around 2 ms.

metrics.name: target worst-case end-to-end latency per flow
metrics.context: Critical-flow deadline used in the IVN evaluation.

metrics.name: maximum relative idle-slope provisioning versus flow-interval baseline
metrics.context: Delay-budget approach may provision up to roughly three times higher idle slope to guarantee deadlines.

limitations.text: The central controller is a potential single point of failure during reservation/setup, although established real-time data paths do not continuously depend on it.
Hard deadline guarantees can require substantial bandwidth overprovisioning relative to less conservative schemes.
Reliable delivery/retransmission is treated as orthogonal to the strict real-time reservation problem, and redundancy mechanisms such as FRER are left for extensions.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for Negotiating strict latency limits for dynamic real-time services in vehicular time-sensitive networks; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full v3 primary text verifies the SOA-to-TSN signaling architecture, network-calculus delay-budget method, 450-subscription/11.1-ms result, 1-ms deadline target, overprovisioning trade-off, controller/SPOF and reliability limitations.

editorial.why_now_note: Dynamic service deployment makes deterministic network configuration a runtime control-plane responsibility rather than a static communication-matrix-only activity.
editorial.rationale: Directly connects application/SOA QoS requests to centralized TSN resource control with worst-case latency validation; one of the strongest network-control architecture items in the intake.
